items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: The Pyramids were built by paid workers, not slaves
items.claim: Who built the Great Pyramid at Giza (c. 2560 BCE)?

options.text: Skilled Egyptian craftsmen and rotating teams of agricultural workers, housed in a workers' town with bakeries and medical care — graves of those who died on the job have been found
Forced labour from Egypt's foreign conquests only
Mercenaries paid in gold from Nubia

items.reveal_title: A workforce, not a chain gang
items.reveal:
Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass excavated the workers' town south of the Giza plateau from the 1980s. They found bakeries producing thousands of loaves daily, fish-processing areas, a medical facility and graves with healed injuries — evidence of long-term care.

Graffiti in the relieving chambers of the Great Pyramid records work-gang names ('Friends of Khufu', 'Drunkards of Menkaure'). Estimates suggest a permanent workforce of perhaps 4,000-5,000 with seasonal labour bringing it to 20,000.

The slave-building myth comes partly from Herodotus (5th century BCE, writing 2,000 years later) and partly from biblical-cinema conflation with the Exodus story.
items.why: The Pyramids as monuments to oppression is a cultural cliché. The archaeological record shows organised state labour with bread rations and beer — not chained slaves under whips.

items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.
